title: Tree planting

definition.text: Transplanting young tree seedlings into the ground, usually for forestry, land reclamation or landscaping.

facts.text: In forestry it is called reforestation where land was recently forested and afforestation where it was not.
Done properly it can regenerate a deforested area, but a planted forest rarely matches the biodiversity and complexity of a natural one.

Outside interests often profit more from fast-growing species such as eucalyptus or pine, whose plantations bring far smaller biodiversity benefits than native forest and are often controversial as offsets.
Many environmentalists argue that only native trees should be planted, to help native ecosystems regrow.
Planted forests covered an estimated 312 million ha in 2025, 8% of all forest area, and grew by 120 million ha since 1990.
Almost all plantation forests (95%) in South America are of introduced species.
Tree-planting initiatives can harm biodiversity, especially in tropical savannas.

contested_note: Plantation offset projects using fast-growing non-native species are described as frequently controversial.

title: Tree planting for climate mitigation
article: Tree planting#Role in climate change mitigation

definition.text: Using new trees to pull carbon dioxide from the air and store it, as a way to limit climate change.

facts.text: Forests act as carbon sinks and take up roughly 25% of human carbon emissions each year.
Forests can switch from sinks to sources: in 2019 they absorbed a third less carbon than in the 1990s because of heat, drought and deforestation.
Avoiding deforestation beats clearing and replanting, which causes irreversible biodiversity loss and soil damage; new forests also take several decades to deliver comparable carbon benefits.
Scientists call protecting and restoring carbon-rich, long-lived ecosystems, especially natural forests, 'the major climate solution'.
An estimate of room for 0.9 billion ha more tree canopy has been criticized; counting albedo and other feedbacks, the area that truly cools is 20-80% lower.
Such planting would store 205 billion tons of carbon only if the trees survive future climate stress to maturity.
Stored carbon must not return to the air through burning or rotting when trees die.
A meta-analysis found mixed-species plantations would store more carbon than single-species ones.

contested_note: The global estimate of land available for climate-cooling tree planting has been criticized as far too high.

definition.text: Planting non-invasive trees that help native species return on their own.

facts.text: A practical approach is to plant tough, fast-growing native species that start rebuilding degraded land.
Farmer-managed natural regeneration, in which farmers protect existing trees instead of replanting, is considered cheaper than ordinary tree planting.

definition.text: The share of incoming sunlight that a surface reflects.

facts.text: It runs from 0, a black body absorbing everything, to 1, a surface reflecting everything.
Fresh snow reflects about 0.9 to 0.95 of visible light, while charcoal reflects about 0.04.
Oceans and most forests have low albedo, while deserts are among the most reflective landforms.
Albedo shapes climate by setting how much radiation a planet absorbs.
Deciduous trees have an albedo of about 0.15 to 0.18 and conifers about 0.09 to 0.15.
Land-use changes such as deforestation, farming and urbanization alter albedo and can perturb Earth's energy balance.

definition.text: The way dark forest canopies absorb more sunlight, partly cancelling the cooling gained when new trees store carbon.

facts.text: Forests have low albedo because they absorb most ultraviolet and visible light for photosynthesis.
In snowy regions, treeless winter albedo is 10% to 50% higher than nearby forest, because snow does not cover trees as readily.
Hadley Centre studies found new tropical and midlatitude forests tended to cool, while high-latitude forests such as in Siberia were neutral or perhaps warming.
For snowy evergreen forests, the albedo effect can be large enough that clearing them causes net cooling.
A 2023 study of 176 flux stations found afforestation may cause moderate warming for about 20 years before turning to significant cooling.
Tropical reforestation helps form clouds that reflect sunlight, while boreal reforestation swaps bright snow for dark canopy and helps the climate less.
Evapotranspiration from trees is usually treated as net cooling, so the overall effect of deforestation depends heavily on local climate.

definition.text: A self-reinforcing loop in which melting snow or ice exposes darker surfaces that absorb more heat and cause more melting.

facts.text: Snow albedo ranges from about 0.9 when fresh to about 0.4 when melting and 0.2 when dirty.
It is one of the main reinforcing climate feedbacks, along with water vapour and the net effect of clouds.
Melting Arctic ice leaves darker water and ground, so less heat is reflected back to space.

title: Human-caused albedo change
article: Albedo#Changes to albedo due to human activities

definition.text: Changes in how much sunlight the land reflects caused by human land use such as cities, farms and deforestation.

facts.text: Urban areas are commonly 0.01–0.02 lower in albedo than nearby cropland, which adds to warming.
Raising urban albedo on purpose can ease the urban heat island effect.
A 2022 estimate found that raising albedo by 0.1 across the world's urban areas would cool as much as absorbing ~44 Gt of CO2.
